name: Karl Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Karl. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say is confidential. Can you start by telling me what a normal working day looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for my father-in-law, Dennis Hale, on his beef and barley place up Stony Lane, about a hundred and twenty suckler cows and three hundred acres. I'm feeding cattle by seven, then it's bedding, fencing, and in summer I'm on the old Massey Ferguson doing whatever Dennis tells me. He's sixty-eight and he still knows ten times what I do.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been farming, and what came before?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three years. Before that I was a scaffolder for twenty, until my shoulder went and the doctor said no more poles. Dennis offered me a wage, and my wife Jo said take it, so here I am. Jo works mornings on reception at the vets in town, and we've got Ryan, who's fifteen, and Ella, who's ten, and a mortgage on the house by the school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never believed it in the first place. A computer can't calve a heifer. I'd say that in the pub and I'd say it to Dennis, and he'd agree with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things stay as they are, which isn't brilliant either. Beef doesn't pay much, Dennis can't pay me more, and nobody's decided who gets the farm. Nothing changing still leaves me working for my father-in-law at forty-three with no say over what happens to the land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, same as now. I'd keep putting a bit aside, about two hundred a month, because we've only got three months or so in the bank. I'd keep my head down and learn the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not because of computers, because of Dennis's age and the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Dennis is sixty-eight. What happens to the farm when he stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody knows. Jo's brother Mark lives in the city and he'll want his share, and I can't buy him out. If they sell, I'm a forty-three-year-old farmhand with a bad shoulder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if beef prices dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sky Sports, then the second car. Then I'd be looking for weekend work, but not on scaffolding, my shoulder won't have it.

I'd say it in the pub and **Dennis** would agree.
think: Things stay as they are, and **beef** still doesn't pay much.
Nobody has decided **who gets the farm** when Dennis stops.
do: Keep working for Dennis and **learning the job**.
Put about **£200 a month** aside, since we only have three months saved.
feel: **Uneasy**, about Dennis's age and the money, not about computers.
S0.quote: Nothing changing still leaves me working for my father-in-law at forty-three with no say over what happens to the land.
fieldNote: His pressure is **succession**: Dennis is sixty-eight and nothing is decided.
A bad shoulder rules out **scaffolding**, his old trade.
Speaks plainly and doesn't trust **technology**, but his worry here isn't about it.

steps.text: Keep feeding and fencing on Dennis's farm as normal
Put about £200 a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not for us, it's for offices. I'd keep my mouth shut more than anything, because I don't know enough about it to argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think it hits Jo before it hits me. Booking appointments and answering the phone, that's exactly what they say goes first. The robots can take their time getting to my cattle, but my wife's job on the vets' front desk is the first thing on their list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the vets do before panicking. I'd cut a few things, the takeaways, the Sky Sports, to be safe. And I'd ask Dennis whether there's more he can pay me if Jo's hours drop, though I know what he'll say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I suppose. Jo's money is what pays the extras.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Jo works on reception at the vets. Is that the kind of work the card talks about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's my worry. She does the phones, the booking, the reminders for jabs. If a computer does all that, they keep one person on the desk, and Jo's part-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you or Dennis ever use any of these tools on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dennis, no chance, he still writes the herd book by hand. Me neither, I don't even use the app on my phone. Maybe Ryan, if he's interested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's gone too far and too fast, and someone should have seen it coming. To Dennis I'd say we need to talk about the farm properly. Online, nothing, I don't do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think Jo's job goes in 2028, simple as that. Then in 2031 the big farms get robots, beef gets cheaper, and Dennis can't compete with his old Massey. By 2031 the robots will be on the big farms, and Dennis will sell before he spends a penny on one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd cut hard, the second car, everything. I'd look for work with the council on the roads, or as a driver, though I'd want something hands-on. And I'd sit Dennis and Jo down and make them decide about the farm before it decides for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like someone's pulled the stool out from under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens on Stony Lane when robots arrive around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Dennis sells, I'm out. A robot farm doesn't need a man still learning the job. And I've only got three months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ryan, who's fifteen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ryan wants to be a mechanic. I'd tell him that's a good shout, because somebody has to fix them. Ella's ten, she's not thinking about any of this.

I'd tell Dennis we need to **talk about the farm** properly.

By **2031** big farms have robots, and Dennis would sell rather than buy one.

Look for **council road work** or driving, something hands-on.
Sit Dennis and Jo down to settle the **farm's future**.

fieldNote: He sees a **double hit**: Jo's job in 2028, then the farm by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time if people use it, and I'd hope the government does something for people like us. At work I'd talk to Dennis more about the future. Online I'd stay quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means Jo's job goes around 2031 instead of 2028, and the robots come in 2034. I'd have a few more years of wages. But I don't think it changes how it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, maybe four hundred a month instead of two. I'd wait a couple of years to see if it's really coming. And I'd push for the family to decide about the farm, sooner not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less sharp than the fast one, but still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. Does that give you anything to work with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five more years of wages is five more years of paying off the mortgage, and that matters more to me than any course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dennis?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him straight that if he wants to keep the farm in the family, we have to plan now. He'll say he'll think about it. He always does.

I'd say I hope the **government** does something for people like us.

fieldNote: He values more **years of wages** over retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time and we'll cross that bridge. I'd probably tell Dennis it's not our problem yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means Dennis will likely have retired by then and the farm question will be settled one way or another. Jo would have years to find something else. It's on my mind, but it's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, honestly. I'd keep working and saving. I'd see what happens before doing anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a long way off, but it's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years out, you'd be in your mid-fifties. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fifty-six with a shoulder that's done, and the mortgage nearly paid. At fifty-six I'd rather be retired than retrained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change about your own work over that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not really. I'd learn the cattle better, that's what I'm still doing anyway.

fieldNote: Ten years lets him **put off** the decision, which suits his resistant style.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Jo's job gone in 2028, and the farm sold by 2031, and me with three months saved and a bad shoulder. What would actually help is my father-in-law deciding who gets the farm before a robot decides for him. And some help from the government for people in their forties who can't go back to their old trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No, I think you've covered it. Just that it's not only about the jobs, it's about the family.

headlineQuote: What would actually help is my father-in-law deciding who gets the farm before a robot decides for him.
portrait: Karl, 43, is a former **scaffolder** who now works for his father-in-law's beef and barley farm.
His wife Jo works part-time on **reception at the vets**, which he sees as the first job to go.
He **never uses AI**, prefers to wait and see, and won't retrain willingly.
The **farm succession** question shadows every picture.
He moves from uneasy to **alarmed** in AGI by 2028, and back to uneasy with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Jo's job and the farm could both go fast.
whatWouldHelp: The **family deciding** who gets the farm early.
**Government help** for people in their forties who can't go back to their trade.
